title: Psalm 60: Have You Rejected Us, O God?
summary: Israel has suffered a military disaster, and the people cry out that God has rejected them and shaken the land. At the center of the psalm God answers from his sanctuary, claiming the tribes of Israel as his own and the surrounding nations as his servants. The psalm ends with a plea for help against Edom and the confidence that with God the people will act with valor.
story: Psalm 60 is the last of the five Miktam psalms (56 to 60), and it shifts from one man's danger to the nation's. The previous psalms traced David's years as a fugitive; this one belongs to his years as king, when Israel fought its neighbors on several fronts. It is a community lament, the kind of prayer the people prayed after defeat, and it contains a divine oracle, a word from God given in the first person. Its second half (verses 5 to 12) was later joined to part of Psalm 57 to form Psalm 108, a sign that Israel's worship reused its prayers in new situations.
historical:
The heading is one of the fullest in the Psalter. It links the psalm to David's wars against Aram-naharaim (Aram of the two rivers, in upper Mesopotamia) and Aram-zobah (an Aramean kingdom north of Damascus), and to Joab's victory over the Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The events are recorded in 2 Samuel 8:3-14 and 1 Chronicles 18:3-13, with related fighting against the Arameans in 2 Samuel 10. The Valley of Salt is usually placed south of the Dead Sea, near the border with Edom. The numbers differ: the heading says Joab struck down 12,000 Edomites; 2 Samuel 8:13 credits David with 18,000 (the Hebrew text there reads Aram, which most translators correct to Edom); and 1 Chronicles 18:12 credits Abishai with 18,000. Interpreters explain this in different ways: separate phases of the campaign, different officers credited for the same victory, or errors in copying numbers, which were easily confused in ancient manuscripts.

A harder question is how a psalm of defeat fits a heading about victory. One view is that while David's main army fought in the north, the Edomites invaded the south and did real damage, and Joab's victory came after this lament. Others think the heading was added later to anchor a national lament in David's reign, and that the psalm's original setting is unknown. The heading also says “for instruction,” a phrase used when David ordered that the lament for Saul and Jonathan be taught to the people of Judah (2 Samuel 1:18). The tune, “The Lily of the Covenant,” is unknown.
cultural:
God's oracle in verses 6 to 8 uses the language of land ownership and royal power. Shechem, west of the Jordan, and the Valley of Succoth, east of it, were places associated with Jacob's return to the land (Genesis 33:17-18), so dividing them is the act of an owner assigning his property. Gilead and Manasseh lay east of the Jordan; Ephraim and Judah were the two strongest tribes west of it. Calling Ephraim God's helmet and Judah his scepter assigns them military and royal roles, and the scepter recalls Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:10).

The neighboring nations fare differently. Moab becomes God's washbasin, the humble bowl in which feet were washed, a menial object. Tossing a sandal over Edom may be a gesture of claiming ownership, since the sandal was used in transactions over land and inheritance (Ruth 4:7), though some read it as simply contemptuous, like throwing a shoe into a corner. Philistia hears a shout of triumph. The “fortified city” of verse 9 is likely an Edomite stronghold; Bozrah and Sela have both been suggested, but the psalm doesn't name it.
literary: The psalm has three parts. Verses 1 to 5 are a lament in which the people describe God's anger in the language of earthquake and drunkenness: the land has been torn open, and the people stagger “from the wine You made us drink,” an early instance of the cup of God's wrath that the prophets develop (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Verses 6 to 8 are God's reply, spoken in the first person “from His sanctuary.” Verses 9 to 12 return to the people's voice, now asking who will lead them to Edom and confessing that human help is worthless. The first and last parts mirror each other: the psalm begins with “You have rejected us” and asks again in verse 10, “Have You not rejected us, O God?” but it ends with confidence that God will trample the enemies.

outline.t: The land shaken and the people staggered
A banner for those who fear God, and a plea for rescue
God's oracle: the land is Mine, the nations serve Me
Who will lead us to Edom?
Human help is worthless; with God we will prevail

doctrines.note: The oracle reasserts God's claim on the tribes and the land. Even when the people feel rejected, the covenant word stands: Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah are his.
God claims not only Israel but Moab, Edom, and Philistia. The nations that threaten Israel are, in the oracle's picture, God's servants and property. His rule is not limited to his own people.
The psalm shows a community praying after defeat. It does not pretend all is well; it names God's anger honestly, asks for restoration, and then listens for God's word before renewing its confidence.

words.note: Zanach, to reject, to cast off. It opens the psalm and returns in verse 10. The word is used of rejecting something as worthless, and in the Psalms it expresses the terrible experience of feeling abandoned by God (Psalm 43:2; 44:9; 74:1; 77:7). Here it is spoken to God directly, as a complaint within the covenant.

Nes, banner, standard, or signal pole. In verse 4 God has raised a banner for those who fear him. A banner was a rallying point in battle, and the Hebrew line is difficult: it may mean a rallying point to flee to for safety, or a banner raised against the bow. God gave himself a similar name after the battle with Amalek, the LORD is my Banner (Exodus 17:15).

Rapha, to heal. The people ask God to heal the land's fractures. The same verb is used of healing bodies, nations, and hearts (Exodus 15:26; 2 Chronicles 7:14). Here the land itself is pictured as wounded, torn open as if by an earthquake.

Teshuah, deliverance, salvation, victory. Verse 11 says literally that the salvation of man is worthless. The word often refers to military victory, and the psalm's point is that victory comes from God rather than from human strength or alliances.

christ: The psalm expresses a people's confidence that God will give them the land he promised and defeat the nations that oppose them. The New Testament reshapes that hope: Jesus, the son of David, receives all authority in heaven and on earth and sends his people to the nations not to conquer them but to make disciples (Matthew 28:18-20). The cup of staggering wine that God gave his people in verse 3 is taken up by Jesus in Gethsemane, when he prays that the cup might pass from him and then drinks it (Mark 14:36). The New Testament does not quote Psalm 60, so these are thematic links. What the psalm says of God's help, that with God his people will act with valor and that human help is worthless without him, the church also confesses of its life in Christ.

hard.q: How can a psalm of defeat carry a heading that celebrates victory, and why do its numbers differ from Samuel and Chronicles?
hard.a: The heading describes a victory over Edom, yet the psalm laments that God has rejected Israel. Some interpreters propose that the lament was written during the campaign, perhaps after an Edomite attack while David's forces were in the north, and that the victory came later in answer. Others think the heading was added by editors who connected a national lament with an episode from David's reign, and that it tells us how the psalm was read rather than when it was written. On the numbers, 12,000 here and 18,000 in Samuel and Chronicles, the proposals include different stages of the same campaign, different commanders credited with the same victory, and scribal errors in copying numbers. None of these explanations is certain, and faithful interpreters differ.

questions: The psalm begins by saying God has rejected his people. Have you ever felt that way? How does this psalm give permission to say it honestly?
Verse 11 says “the help of man is worthless.” Where are you tempted to rely on human help instead of God's?
The psalm moves from complaint to listening to God's word before it ends in confidence. How can listening change what we pray?
